title: Appeals to the Board of Supervisors: who appealed and who won
question: How many appeals of planning decisions did the Board uphold, reject or never vote on, and does that differ by kind of appeal, district, kind of project, year or appellant?
finding: Of 251 appeals filed with the Board from 2015 to 2026, 164 were decided by a vote and 40 (24.4%) were upheld - 24 overturning the decision and 16 approving the project again under the Board’s own conditions; 87 never reached a vote. Conditional-use appeals were upheld in 59.6% of 47 decided and environmental-review appeals in 12.0% of 100; named organizations (24.7% of 73) and individuals (25.0% of 72) fared alike, and no district with 20 or more decided appeals differs from what its mix of appeal kinds predicts by more than chance.
how: An appeal is one hearing file. The Board records its decision on sibling motion files - one affirming the decision appealed, one reversing it, one on findings - and adopts one and tables the others; the last affirming or reversing motion to pass decides the outcome here. “Approved again under the Board’s own conditions” means the adopted motion both disapproves the Planning Commission’s approval and approves the same project with different or added conditions. “No vote” covers appeals the Clerk filed without a hearing, appeals withdrawn, and hearings where every motion was tabled. The district is the one printed in the title, or else the district of the address in the title. The kind of project is read from the words of the title with the same rules as the planning-applications screen. The appellant is classed from the title’s “(Appellant: ...)” text: a named body, individuals, or both. “Expected” gives each decided appeal the citywide upheld rate for its kind (conditional use, environmental, map); a gap is called beyond chance at about the 1-in-100 level. Rates are printed only on 20 or more decided appeals.
limits: The titles never name the project sponsor, so who was on the other side is not in this table. An appeal “filed without a hearing” may have been late, withdrawn or found not to qualify: the record read here does not say which. 30 of the 79 conditional-use appeals were filed without a hearing, so those that reach a vote are a selected group, and that alone could explain part of the gap with environmental appeals. Small projects and large ones, and districts with many or few appeals, are not alike. The kind of project is a keyword reading and puts many titles in “other”. A difference between areas, or between groups of cases, is not proof of bias. Areas differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply, object or appeal at all.
